newsitem.title: PERU: Peruvian police bar Mothers from Lima siege site.
newsitem.headline: Peruvian police bar Mothers from Lima siege site.

text.p: Peruvian police on Saturday blocked a delegation from one of Latin America's most famous human rights groups from paying a visit to 72 men held hostage by Marxist rebels at the Japanese ambassador's home in Lima.

Three representatives of the Mothers of the Plaza de Mayo, famous for opposing Argentina's military dictatorship in the 1970s, were turned away at a police cordon blocking access to a street leading to the residence.
They left two hours later but vowed to return on Sunday to try again to gain access to the compound where Tupac Amaru Revolutionary Movement (MRTA) rebels are holding hostages for the 67th day.
The band of about 15 MRTA rebels seized the mansion and hundreds of cocktail party guests on Dec. 17. All but 72 have been released.
The Mothers arrived in Lima earlier this week, sporting their trademark white scarves over their white hair, in hopes of meeting with hostages as well as some of about 400 imprisoned MRTA members.
But the group was snubbed on Friday when they went to the Government Palace to meet with President Alberto Fujimori and no one answered the door.

As the delegation squared off with police toting automatic weapons, a pentacostal church group staged a march by 2,000 people, mostly children, on streets around the mansion in Lima's upscale San Isidro district.
Waving flags and carrying signs reading "Jesus Visits the Hostages" and "Christ Liberty," the children marched to express their solidarity with the hostages, according to organisers.
As pentacostals marched and Mothers protested beyond police lines, three members of the guarantors commission mediating the crisis met for more than two hours inside the residence.
Archbishop Juan Luis Cipriani, Canada's ambassador Anthony Vincent and the Red Cross' Michel Minnig left the mansion at 6:20 p.m. local time (2320 GMT) without speaking to reporters.
